concepts.name: Chemical Reaction
concepts.text: A chemical reaction is a process where the nature and identity of a substance changes, occurring whenever a chemical change takes place in matter.

source_span.quote:
Whenever a chemical
change occurs, we can say that a chemical reaction has taken place.

concepts.name: Reactants
concepts.text: Reactants are the substances that undergo chemical change in a reaction and are written on the left-hand side of a chemical equation.

source_span.quote:
The substances that undergo chemical change in the reaction (1.1),
magnesium and oxygen, are the reactants.

concepts.name: Products
concepts.text: Products are the new substances formed during a chemical reaction, written on the right-hand side of a chemical equation.

source_span.quote:
The new substance is
magnesium oxide, formed during the reaction, as a product.

concepts.name: Word-equation
concepts.text: A word-equation represents a chemical reaction by showing the transformation of reactants to products in sentence form using words rather than chemical symbols.

source_span.quote:
A word-equation shows change of reactants to products through an
arrow placed between them.

concepts.name: Chemical Equation
concepts.text: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using chemical formulae instead of words for a more concise and useful representation.

source_span.quote:
A chemical equation represents a
chemical reaction.

concepts.name: Skeletal Chemical Equation
concepts.text: A skeletal chemical equation is an initial chemical equation written using chemical formulae but before it is balanced, where the number of atoms of each element may not be equal on both sides.

source_span.quote:
Such a chemical equation is a skeletal
chemical equation for a reaction.

concepts.name: Balanced Chemical Equation
concepts.text: A balanced chemical equation is one where the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the arrow, satisfying the law of conservation of mass.

source_span.quote:
As the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of
the arrow, Eq. (1.3) is a balanced chemical equation.

concepts.name: Law of Conservation of Mass
concepts.text: The law stating that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, meaning the total mass of elements in products equals the total mass in reactants.

source_span.quote:
Recall the law of conservation of mass that you studied in Class IX; mass
can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

periods.title: Introduction to Chemical Reactions
objectives: Define a chemical reaction and identify examples of chemical change
Distinguish reactants from products in a given reaction
Represent a chemical reaction using a word-equation
periods.sequencing_rationale: This period lays the conceptual foundation by introducing what a chemical reaction is and how it can be represented in the simplest form (words) before moving to symbolic representation. Students must grasp reactants/products conceptually before they can write formal equations.

periods.title: From Words to Symbols: Writing Chemical Equations
objectives: Convert word-equations into chemical equations using formulae
Understand the purpose and advantages of using chemical equations over word-equations
Identify a skeletal chemical equation and recognize why it needs balancing
periods.sequencing_rationale: Building on the previous period's word-equations, students now learn the symbolic representation, which is a direct progression from qualitative to quantitative/symbolic literacy. Introducing the skeletal equation sets up the need for balancing in the next period.

periods.title: Balancing Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
objectives: State and explain the law of conservation of mass
Understand why chemical equations must be balanced
Practice balancing simple skeletal equations to form balanced chemical equations
Verify atom counts of elements on both sides of an equation
periods.sequencing_rationale: This period logically follows the introduction of skeletal equations, providing the conceptual justification (conservation of mass) and the practical skill (balancing) needed to complete the equation-writing process. Since balancing requires hands-on numerical practice, it needs a longer, focused session.

teaching_plan.planning_rationale: The content covers a tightly connected conceptual progression: understanding what a chemical reaction is, representing it in words, converting to symbolic chemical equations, and finally balancing those equations using the law of conservation of mass. For beginner Grade 10 students, each stage requires dedicated time to build understanding before advancing — rushing word-equations and balancing into one session would overwhelm learners new to symbolic chemistry. Three periods allow a natural build-up: (1) conceptual foundation, (2) symbolic representation, and (3) the more skill-intensive balancing practice, which needs a longer session due to its hands-on, iterative nature.

periods.mentor_moment: Encourage students to connect chemistry to their everyday lives - when they see rusting, fermenting, or cooking as chemical reactions, the subject stops feeling abstract and becomes something they observe daily. Use their own home examples as much as possible to build ownership of the concept.
periods.teacher_script: Begin by asking students to recall changes they see every day - milk turning sour, an iron nail rusting, food being cooked. Explain that a chemical reaction is a process where the nature and identity of a substance changes, occurring whenever a chemical change takes place in matter. Emphasize that this is different from just a physical change like ice melting, because in a chemical reaction, entirely new substances form. Introduce the burning of magnesium ribbon in air as a classic example: point out the dazzling white flame and the white powder that forms - this shows visible signs of a chemical reaction. Then explain that every chemical reaction has a starting point and an ending point. The substances that undergo chemical change in a reaction are called reactants, and they are written on the left-hand side of a chemical equation. The new substances formed during a chemical reaction are called products, written on the right-hand side. Show how we can represent this transformation in sentence form using words rather than chemical symbols - this is called a word-equation. Work through the magnesium example as a word-equation: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium Oxide. Ask students to identify reactants and products in this equation. Then discuss other daily-life examples: milk left at room temperature during summers undergoing fermentation, iron tawa/pan/nail rusting when exposed to humid atmosphere, grapes fermenting, food being cooked, food digestion in the body, and respiration - all are chemical reactions happening in daily life. Have students attempt to write simple word-equations for a couple of these examples.

WORD-EQUATION: Reactants (in words) -> Products (in words)

periods.mentor_moment: When introducing chemical formulae, go slow with the symbols - many students confuse subscripts and coefficients at this stage. Use plenty of atom-counting practice before moving to balancing so students build confidence rather than fear of equations.
periods.teacher_script: Start by reviewing the word-equation from the last class: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium Oxide. Ask students how chemists might write this more concisely. Introduce that a chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using chemical formulae instead of words for a more concise and useful representation. Convert the word-equation into a chemical equation using formulae: Mg + O2 -> MgO. Discuss why chemists prefer chemical equations: they are shorter, universally understood regardless of language, and show exact quantities and formulae involved. Now introduce the idea that not every chemical equation written straight from formulae is correct as it stands. Show the example of iron reacting with water: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2, an unbalanced chemical equation showing the reaction between iron and water. Explain that this is called a skeletal chemical equation - an initial chemical equation written using chemical formulae but before it is balanced, where the number of atoms of each element may not be equal on both sides. Have students count atoms of Fe, H, and O on both sides to discover the mismatch themselves. Point out the misconception that a chemical equation written with chemical formulae is automatically balanced without checking if atom counts match on both sides - stress that this is NOT true, and balancing is a necessary next step, which we will do in the next class.
periods.blackboard_notes:
CHEMICAL EQUATION: reaction shown using chemical formulae (concise, universal)
Word equation: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium Oxide
Chemical equation: Mg + O2 -> MgO
SKELETAL CHEMICAL EQUATION: formulae used but NOT balanced
Example: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 (unbalanced - count atoms!)
CAUTION: writing formulae does NOT mean it's automatically balanced!

periods.mentor_moment: Balancing equations can frustrate students at first - remind them it is a puzzle-solving skill that improves only with repeated practice. Celebrate small wins, like a student correctly balancing their first equation, to build their confidence before moving to more complex reactions.
periods.teacher_script: Begin by revisiting the skeletal equation from last class and the atom counts students found - they should notice mismatches. Introduce the law of conservation of mass: mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, meaning the total mass of elements in products equals the total mass in reactants. Explain that this scientific principle is why every chemical equation must be balanced - if atoms disappeared or appeared out of nowhere, it would violate this fundamental law of nature. Define a balanced chemical equation as one where the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the arrow, satisfying the law of conservation of mass. Walk through balancing the iron-water equation step by step: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2, showing how coefficients are added (never changing subscripts) until atom counts match. Then work through the zinc-sulphuric acid reaction: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2, the reaction between zinc and sulphuric acid to produce zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas, representing a balanced chemical equation - have students verify it is already balanced by counting Zn, H, S, O atoms on both sides. Give students 2-3 more skeletal equations to practice balancing on their own, then have them verify atom counts on both sides as a final check for each.
periods.blackboard_notes:
LAW OF CONSERVATION OF MASS: mass neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; total mass reactants = total mass products
BALANCED CHEMICAL EQUATION: atoms of each element equal on both sides of arrow
Example 1: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2 (balanced)
Example 2: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (already balanced)
Steps: 1) Count atoms each side 2) Add coefficients 3) Recount to verify

checkpoint_questions.question: Verify that Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 is a balanced equation by counting atoms of each element on both sides.

source_spans.quote: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Left side: 1 Zn, 2 H, 1 S, 4 O. Right side: 1 Zn, 1 S, 4 O (in ZnSO4) + 2 H (in H2) = 1 Zn, 2 H, 1 S, 4 O. Both sides match, so it is balanced.

activities.title: Atom Counting Lab: Checking for Balance
materials: Molecular model kits or colored beads/balls representing atoms
instructions: Give each group a skeletal chemical equation (e.g., Fe + H2O → Fe3O4 + H2) and a set of atom-model beads.
Have students build physical models of reactant and product molecules using the beads to represent atoms.
Ask students to count and record the number of atoms of each element on both the reactant and product sides.
Guide students to add coefficients (multiply molecules) to make the atom counts equal on both sides, rearranging bead models as needed.
Once balanced, have students verify that total atoms of each element match on both sides and discuss how this reflects the law of conservation of mass.

long_answer.question: Discuss the concept of a chemical reaction, distinguishing between reactants and products, and illustrate your answer with the example of magnesium burning in oxygen. Also represent this reaction as a word-equation.
long_answer.model_answer:
A chemical reaction is a process where the nature and identity of a substance changes, occurring whenever a chemical change takes place in matter. In any chemical reaction, there are two key components: reactants and products. Reactants are the substances that undergo chemical change in a reaction and are written on the left-hand side of a chemical equation, while products are the new substances formed during the reaction, written on the right-hand side. 

A good illustration is the combustion of magnesium metal in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Here, magnesium and oxygen are the reactants, since they are the substances present before the reaction and undergo change. Magnesium oxide is the product, since it is the new substance formed as a result of the reaction. This reaction is accompanied by a dazzling white flame and the formation of a white powder, both visible signs of chemical change.

As a word-equation, this reaction can be represented as: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide. This word-equation shows the transformation of reactants (magnesium and oxygen) to the product (magnesium oxide) in sentence form using words rather than chemical symbols.

long_answer.question: Describe the process of converting a word-equation into a chemical equation using formulae. Use the reaction between zinc and sulphuric acid as an example, and explain the difference between a skeletal equation and a balanced chemical equation in this context.
long_answer.model_answer:
Converting a word-equation into a chemical equation involves replacing the words for reactants and products with their respective chemical formulae. For example, the word-equation 'Zinc + Sulphuric acid → Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen' can be converted into a chemical equation using formulae: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2.

When first written using formulae, before checking whether the atoms balance, the equation is called a skeletal chemical equation — an initial chemical equation written using chemical formulae but before it is balanced, where the number of atoms of each element may not be equal on both sides. Once the atoms of each element are verified to be equal on both sides of the arrow, satisfying the law of conservation of mass, it becomes a balanced chemical equation. In this case, Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2 represents the reaction between zinc and sulphuric acid to produce zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas, representing a balanced chemical equation, since there is one zinc atom, two hydrogen atoms, one sulphur atom, and four oxygen atoms on each side.

solution_steps: Left side (reactants): Zn = 1 atom, H = 2 atoms (from H2SO4), S = 1 atom, O = 4 atoms.
Right side (products): Zn = 1 atom (from ZnSO4), S = 1 atom (from ZnSO4), O = 4 atoms (from ZnSO4), H = 2 atoms (from H2).
Comparing both sides: Zn (1=1), H (2=2), S (1=1), O (4=4) — all atom counts match on both sides.
Since the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides, this confirms the equation is balanced and satisfies the law of conservation of mass.

long_answer.question: Explain the law of conservation of mass and describe, using the examples of the zinc-sulphuric acid reaction and the iron-water reaction, how this law is verified through the process of balancing chemical equations.
long_answer.model_answer:
The law of conservation of mass states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, meaning the total mass of elements in products equals the total mass in reactants. This principle underlies the requirement that all chemical equations must be balanced: a balanced chemical equation is one where the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the arrow, satisfying the law of conservation of mass.

Consider the reaction between zinc and sulphuric acid to produce zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2. This is an example of a balanced chemical equation, since counting the atoms shows one zinc atom, two hydrogen atoms, one sulphur atom, and four oxygen atoms on each side — verifying that mass is conserved.

In contrast, consider the unbalanced chemical equation showing the reaction between iron and water: Fe + H2O → Fe3O4 + H2. Here, the number of atoms of iron, hydrogen, and oxygen are not equal on both sides, so this is a skeletal (unbalanced) equation. To make it consistent with the law of conservation of mass, coefficients must be added until the atoms of each element balance on both sides, at which point it becomes a proper balanced chemical equation. This process of balancing equations is essentially how chemists verify, at the level of individual reactions, that the law of conservation of mass holds true.

short_answer.question: The equation Fe + H2O → Fe3O4 + H2 is an unbalanced chemical equation showing the reaction between iron and water. Explain what steps you would take conceptually to verify and balance this equation.
short_answer.model_answer: To balance this skeletal equation, I would first count the number of atoms of each element (Fe, H, O) on both the reactant and product sides. Since the equation is unbalanced, the atom counts will not match on both sides. I would then add appropriate coefficients in front of the reactants and/or products so that the number of atoms of iron, hydrogen, and oxygen are equal on both sides of the arrow, without changing the chemical formulae themselves. Finally, I would recount the atoms on both sides to verify the equation is now balanced, satisfying the law of conservation of mass.

gaps.remediation: Explicitly teach students the distinction between a skeletal equation and a balanced equation: emphasize that writing correct chemical formulae for reactants and products only produces a skeletal equation, which may not have equal atom counts on both sides. Provide guided practice where students first write the skeletal equation, then systematically tally the number of atoms of each element on the left- and right-hand sides in a table, and only add coefficients to balance the equation once a mismatch is found. Reinforce this with the law of conservation of mass as the underlying justification, using multiple examples (including polyatomic reactants/products) where an unbalanced skeletal equation is deliberately shown alongside its correctly balanced counterpart so students can compare and internalize the checking process as a mandatory step, not an assumption.
